Backpressure is a control mechanism in streaming and concurrent systems that prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer.

## Problem It Solves

When a producer emits items faster than a downstream consumer can process them, without backpressure the intermediate buffer grows without bounds, consuming memory until the process runs out and crashes. Backpressure provides feedback from the consumer back to the producer, allowing the producer to slow its emission rate to match the consumer's processing capacity.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues with Blocking

The producer writes items to a queue with a fixed maximum size. Once the queue is full, the producer blocks (waits) until the consumer drains enough items to make room. This is simple and synchronous but can cause thread stalls if the producer and consumer run on the same threads.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a fixed number (N) of items before requiring the consumer to grant more credits. This is common in network protocols and reactive systems — the producer only sends when it has available credits, and the consumer refills the credit pool as it processes items. It decouples producer and consumer timing and works well across network boundaries.

### Reactive Pull (Request-Driven)

Instead of the producer pushing items, the consumer explicitly requests items from the producer (often via a `request(n)` method). The producer only emits what was requested. This is the foundation of reactive-stream models (such as Reactive Streams or Project Reactor) and gives the consumer precise control over its processing rate.

## Characteristics

- **Prevents memory exhaustion**: Stops unbounded buffer growth.
- **Couples producer pacing to consumer capacity**: The producer naturally adapts to downstream speed.
- **Adds latency**: If a consumer is very slow, the producer will wait; this is the trade-off.
- **Requires bidirectional communication**: The consumer must signal the producer somehow (via queue full state, explicit credits, or pull requests).
